recipes.name: Chai Po (Sweet Preserved Radish)
recipes.flavorProfile: Salty, sweet and chewy, with a crunch.
recipes.healthBenefit: Used by the spoonful for flavor; it is salty.

ingredients.cutPrep: peeled and cut in thick strips

ingredients.prepNote: part for the radish, part drawn out with the water and squeezed away; 2.5% of the radish weight

instructions: Toss the radish with the salt and leave it overnight under a weight. Squeeze out and pour away the liquid.
Dry the strips in the sun, or in a 60 C (140 F) oven, for 1 to 2 days until leathery.
Toss them with the sugar until it melts into a light syrup, pack into a jar and cure in the refrigerator 2 to 3 days before using. Chop fine to use.

nutritionHighlights.note: High: the radish is cured in salt, so a little goes a long way.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipedia, Chai poh for every amount and step; gives sweet chai poh as 2 to 3% salt and 5 to 10% sugar by radish weight; the recipe pages it cites could not be opened.

recipes.name: Luk Chin Nuea (Thai Beef Balls)
recipes.flavorProfile: Springy, savory and peppery, seasoned with fish sauce.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lean beef brings protein, iron and zinc.
instructions: Cube the beef and chill it until very cold.
Grind the cold beef very fine in a food processor with the fish sauce, salt and pepper.
Add the corn starch, baking powder and ice water bit by bit and process until a sticky, smooth paste forms. Chill 1 hour.
Squeeze balls of about 18 g through your fist into warm water, then simmer gently 8 to 10 minutes until they float and spring back. Drain. The batch makes about 30 balls.

citations.source: Cooking with Morgane, Thai Beef Balls

recipes.curationNote: Cooking with Morgane, Thai Beef Balls for every amount and step; 500 g beef, 15 g corn starch, 10 g salt, 1 tbsp fish sauce, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp ground pepper, 50 ml water for 30 balls; the page sends the method to its video, so the steps keep the usual cold grind, beat and simmer.

recipes.name: Kaep Moo (Pork Rinds)
recipes.flavorProfile: Puffed, crackly and salty, with a rich pork taste.
recipes.healthBenefit: Mostly protein from collagen and fat; a garnish rather than a main source of anything.

ingredients.prepNote: 1/2 tsp, tossed with the raw pieces

instructions: Cut the pork skin into bite sized pieces and toss them in a bowl with the salt and vinegar.

Put the pieces in a wide pan with 120 ml (1/2 cup) water over medium heat. The skin takes up the water, then gives up its fat; keep cooking in that fat until the pieces turn golden, about 1 hour 10 minutes in all.
Leave the rinds sitting in the rendered fat for 1 hour.
Heat again and fry a second time until golden, puffed and crisp.
Drain well in a colander. One serving is 20 g.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the fat the pork skin renders as it cooks.

citations.source: Hungry in Thailand, Hot and Spicy Pork Rinds

recipes.curationNote: Hungry in Thailand, Hot and Spicy Pork Rinds (plain rinds part) for every amount and step; the plain rinds use 1 kg pork skin, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp vinegar and 1 cup water and fry in the fat the skin gives up; ours is half that batch. The spice blend tossed on at the end is a separate seasoning and is left out of this plain base.

recipes.name: See Ew Dam Waan (Sweet Dark Soy Sauce)
recipes.flavorProfile: Thick, dark, sweet and salty, with a burnt caramel edge.
recipes.healthBenefit: Used by the spoonful for colour and sweetness; it is high in sugar and salt.

ingredients.prepNote: about 1 1/3 cups (330 ml), wheat free; soy sauce weighs about 1.08 g per ml

instructions: Put the water and brown sugar in a heavy pan and bring to a boil over high heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves.
Turn the heat to medium low and leave it to bubble without stirring until it turns as dark as strong coffee.
Take the pan off the heat and pour in the soy sauce slowly; it will foam up hard.
Stir until it is smooth and thick like molasses. Cool, then keep it in a clean jar in the fridge for about a month.

nutritionHighlights.note: High, from the caramelised brown sugar.

citations.source: Pranee's Thai Kitchen, Dark Soy Sauce

recipes.curationNote: Pranee's Thai Kitchen, Dark Soy Sauce for every amount and step; 1/4 cup water, 1 cup dark brown sugar and 1/2 cup wheat free soy sauce make 3/4 cup (12 tbsp); ours makes 33 tbsp, so 2.75 times the batch.

recipes.name: Sriracha (Fermented Chilli Sauce)
recipes.healthBenefit: Fresh chillies bring vitamin C; used by the spoonful.

ingredients.prepNote: red jalapeno or serrano peppers, stemmed

instructions: Blend the peppers, garlic, vinegar and water until smooth.
Strain into a heavy pot through a sieve that is not too fine, pressing out as much liquid as you can; some pulp going through gives the sauce its body.
Whisk in the sugar and salt and bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring now and then.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until it thickens and cooks down to about 2 1/4 cups (35 tbsp).
Cool completely and keep in a clean glass jar in the fridge, using a clean spoon each time. Let it rest 2 days before using so the garlic mellows. It keeps about a month, or it can be frozen.

nutritionHighlights.note: Fresh red chillies are rich in vitamin C, though some is lost in cooking.
From the salt; a tablespoon carries a good deal of it.

recipes.curationNote: SheSimmers, Homemade Sriracha for every amount and step; makes about 4 cups (64 tbsp): 24 oz red jalapeno or serrano peppers, 8 oz peeled garlic, 4 fl oz white vinegar, 12 fl oz water, 16 oz sugar, 6 tbsp salt, blended, strained, then simmered down to about 4 cups; no fermenting. Scaled by 35/64 to our 35 tablespoons.

recipes.name: Kratiam Dong (Thai Pickled Garlic)
recipes.healthBenefit: Garlic, softened by pickling; eaten a few cloves at a time.

ingredients.cutPrep: small whole heads, outer skin rubbed off
ingredients.prepNote: small whole heads; roots trimmed, outer skin peeled, washed
the share taken up; the brine holds 150 g (3/4 cup)
the share taken up; the brine holds 27 g (1 1/2 tbsp)
the share taken up; the jar holds 120 ml (1/2 cup)

instructions: Trim the roots off the garlic heads, peel away the loose outer skin and wash them. Pack them into a clean jar.
Boil 240 ml (1 cup) water, 120 ml (1/2 cup) white vinegar, 150 g (3/4 cup) sugar and 27 g (1 1/2 tbsp) salt hard, then let the brine cool.
Pour the cooled brine over the garlic to cover, close the jar and leave it in a shady place for about 1 month before using. It keeps about a year.
Only about a quarter of the brine is eaten with the garlic, so only that share is counted.

nutritionHighlights.note: Pickling mellows the sharp sulfur compounds of raw garlic.

citations.source: JIRCAS, Thai fermented foods database: Kra tiam dorng

recipes.curationNote: JIRCAS Thai fermented foods database, Kra tiam dorng (pickled garlic) for every amount and step; per 1 kg fresh garlic bulbs: sugar 1 1/2 cups, vinegar 1 cup, salt 3 tbsp, water 2 cups; brine boiled, cooled and poured over, left in shade about 1 month. Ours is half that batch; about a quarter of the brine is counted as eaten.

recipes.name: Pla Ra (Fermented Fish)
recipes.flavorProfile: Very salty, pungent and deeply savoury.
recipes.healthBenefit: A seasoning used by the spoonful; it is very salty.

ingredients.cutPrep: small freshwater fish, scaled, gutted and cleaned
ingredients.prepNote: stands in for the gourami, snakehead, catfish and small fish used in Isan

instructions: Mix the cleaned fish with the salt, cover and leave it overnight.
Mix in the rice bran, pack it tightly into a clay or glass jar, close it and leave it in a cool, dark place for 4 to 6 months, or longer for a stronger flavour. It makes about 1.5 kg.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the salt; very salty, so a little goes a long way.

citations.source: Thailand Foundation, Pla ra: Thai fermented fish

recipes.curationNote: Thailand Foundation, Pla ra: pla ra nua is freshwater fish, salt and rice bran at 4 to 1 to 1, fermented about 4 to 6 months in a closed jar, and generally at least 6 months. The page gives no step by step method; the overnight salting first follows Wikipedia. One serving is one tablespoon, about 18 g.
